3. For reactors in series, the output of one becomes the input of the next

(R) 1 m³ PFR followed by 1 m³ CSTR (total volume 2 m³)

- PFRs always give higher conversion than CSTRs of the same volume
- For reactors in series, the order matters (PFR followed by CSTR is less efficient than CSTR followed by PFR)
- Larger total volume generally means higher conversion

Configuration Q has the same total volume (4 m³) but is all CSTR, which is less efficient than having some PFR, so X_Q < X_P.

Configurations R and S both have 2 m³ total volume, but R has a PFR followed by CSTR while S has two CSTRs in series. For first-order reactions, two CSTRs in series perform better than a single CSTR of the same total volume, but not as well as a PFR followed by CSTR. So X_S < X_R.

Comparing Q and S: Q has twice the volume but is a single CSTR, while S has two CSTRs in series. For first-order reactions, two CSTRs in series perform better than a single CSTR of the same total volume. However, Q has twice the volume of S, which would tend to increase conversion. Since Q has twice the volume of S, if the flow rate is the same, τ_Q = 2τ_S. For first-order reactions, two equal-sized CSTRs in series with total residence time τ will give higher conversion than a single CSTR with residence time τ. However, Q has twice the residence time of S, which complicates the comparison.
